Help given by one country or organisation to another, such as money, food, medicine or expertise.
A person who has left their country and asked another country for protection as a refugee.
The variety of plant and animal life in a particular place or ecosystem.
Gases such as carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere, mainly by burning fossil fuels. They trap heat and cause global warming.
The total amount of greenhouse gases produced by a person, product, organisation or country.
A long-term change in average weather patterns. Today it is mainly caused by human activity increasing greenhouse gases.
Protecting and managing natural environments and wildlife so they are not damaged or lost.
When corals lose the algae that live inside them, usually because the sea is too warm, turning them white and putting them at risk of dying.
The amount of money needed to pay for basic needs such as housing, food, energy and transport.
Money owed. Many lower-income countries owe large debts, which can limit spending on health and education.
Cutting down or clearing forests, often for farming, logging, mining or building.
When land in dry areas becomes more like a desert, often because of drought, overgrazing and deforestation.
Improving people's quality of life and standard of living, including their wealth, health and education.
When people are forced to leave their homes, for example by conflict, disaster or development projects.
A long period with much less rainfall than normal, leading to water shortages.
Sudden shaking of the ground caused by the movement of tectonic plates.
A community of plants and animals and the environment they live in, all linked together.
A natural warming of the Pacific Ocean every few years that changes weather patterns around the world. La Niña is the cooling phase.
Having reliable, affordable access to enough energy.
Weather that is much more severe than usual, such as heatwaves, very heavy rain or powerful storms.
A severe shortage of food across a whole area, causing widespread hunger and death.
When water covers land that is normally dry, often from heavy rain, rivers overflowing or storm surges.
When everyone has reliable access to enough affordable, nutritious food. Food insecurity is when they do not.
Fuels such as coal, oil and gas formed from ancient plants and animals. Burning them releases carbon dioxide.
Gross domestic product: the total value of goods and services produced by a country in a year.
A large, slow-moving mass of ice on land. Many are shrinking because of global warming.
The growing connections between countries through trade, investment, travel, culture and technology.
A natural event that threatens people and property. It becomes a disaster when it causes serious harm.
A period of unusually hot weather lasting several days.
The basic rights and freedoms that belong to every person, such as freedom from torture and the right to education.
A situation where many people urgently need help with food, water, shelter or medical care.
The original inhabitants of a place, with their own cultures, languages and links to the land.
Differences in wealth, opportunities or quality of life between people or places.
A general rise in prices over time, which reduces what money can buy.
The basic structures a place needs to function, such as roads, power, water supply and communications.
A mass of rock, earth or mud moving quickly down a slope.
The average number of years a person is expected to live. It is often used as a development indicator.
The movement of people from one place to another to live, either within a country or between countries.
Actions that reduce the causes of a problem, such as cutting greenhouse gas emissions to limit climate change.
Changing how we live to cope with a problem, such as building flood defences as sea levels rise.
A seasonal wind change bringing very heavy rain, especially in South Asia from June to September.
Materials from the natural world that people use, such as water, minerals, timber and fossil fuels.
The build-up of plastic waste in the environment, especially in rivers and oceans.
Harmful substances released into the air, water or land.
Changes in the number of people living in a place, caused by births, deaths and migration.
Not having enough money or resources to meet basic needs such as food, shelter and clean water.
How good people's lives are, including health, safety, education, environment and happiness.
A person forced to leave their country to escape war, persecution or disaster.
Energy from sources that will not run out, such as the sun, wind and flowing water.
Relating to the countryside rather than towns and cities.
Penalties, such as trade restrictions, that one or more countries place on another to pressure it to change its behaviour.
The average height of the sea increasing, mainly because of melting ice and warming water expanding.
A country's full right and power to govern itself and its territory.
The network of producers, transport and sellers that moves a product from raw materials to customers.
Meeting the needs of people today without damaging the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
A tax on imported goods, which makes them more expensive.
The huge slabs of the Earth's crust that move slowly and cause earthquakes and volcanoes where they meet.
Travelling for pleasure. It is an important source of jobs and income for many places.
Buying and selling goods and services, especially between countries.
A powerful spinning storm that forms over warm oceans. It is called a hurricane, typhoon or cyclone depending on where it forms.
A series of huge sea waves, usually caused by an undersea earthquake.
When people who want to work cannot find a job.
The growth in the proportion of people living in towns and cities.
An opening in the Earth's crust where magma, ash and gases escape.

When there is not enough safe water to meet people's needs.
An uncontrolled fire spreading through vegetation, made more likely by heat and drought.
